Remember how rightfully angry people got in 2020  when politicians like Gavin Newsom restricted access to churches because of a potential threat to public safety, because our faith matters more than our comfort?

During COVID, Gavin Newsom and countless other politicians imposed strict, long term bans on indoor church services and called them “nonessential” in order to “keep people safe.”

Whether it’s the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels in Los Angeles or the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in

To say it again—forcibly closing ANY religious site, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Western Wall, the al Aqsa Mosque, or anywhere else over “safety” is always wrong.

Religious liberty matters always, but perhaps even more during times of conflict, violence, and war.

Imagine telling the Apostle Peter, “welllll Christianity is illegal in Rome, so you really shouldn’t go just for your safety, tbh.”

My heart is absolutely broken over the news from Jerusalem today that the Israeli government has denied access to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre to Cardinal Pizzaballa and 4 other priests to celebrate a private mass on behalf of the faithful denied the right to gather on Palm Sunday, and yours should be too.

This is an unprecedented move that has ramifications and impact worldwide, and matters deeply in our continued fight for religious freedom around the world.

Today, take a moment to look at this photo, taken in March 1945 in the rubble of the partially destroyed Cologne Cathedral.

Here, soldiers gathered around the altar to celebrate the Passion of Christ and be united with Him in the Eucharist, even under the threat of violence and death.

Bombs were quite literally dropping everywhere around these faithful Christians, but nothing mattered more to them then than the holy mass.

We should never wish *for* violence or dangerous circumstances in the world—but if bombs are being dropped on Palm Sunday or Easter Sunday or any other day of the year… there’s no place I’d rather be than on my knees in front of the tabernacle, holding the very Holy Presence of our Savior Jesus Christ in the Eucharist.
